name: Running Dry
description: Shelf Tier 1 expression meaning to operate without any augmentation active — either because you can't afford the upkeep charges on your chrome, your BCI subscription has lapsed, or you've deliberately gone dark to avoid detection. 'Running dry' is not the same as having no augmentation; it specifically describes the state of having chrome that is currently inactive, throttled, or locked out, which on the Shelf is a common condition tied directly to poverty cycles and corporate subscription models for aug maintenance. The term carries no shame in Tier 1 usage — it's a simple statement of circumstance — but in Tier 3-4 it reads as embarrassing, signaling financial precarity.
cultural_impact: The prevalence of 'running dry' on the Shelf has fueled a significant black-market industry in cracked aug firmware and unlicensed maintenance rigs that keep chrome running without corporate subscription fees, making it a central term in discussions about augmentation access inequality. The phrase has become a rallying point for aug-rights advocates arguing that locking life-sustaining chrome behind subscription models constitutes a form of corporate bodily control.
key_figures: Corponation Helion Integrated (primary subscription aug provider, antagonist in this context)
locations: Dry March rally point, Shelf District 11 plaza
Helion Integrated service kiosks (sites of frequent protest)
story_hooks: A Shelf medic who runs dry for three weeks every month when her chrome subscription lapses is the only person who can perform a critical surgery — but her hands won't be steady without her augmented motor stabilizers, and she can't afford to reactivate them.

Helion Integrated is quietly extending the 'dry window' — the period before locked aug hardware causes physical harm — testing how long Shelf residents will tolerate it before the situation becomes politically explosive.

Someone is selling a firmware crack that keeps aug hardware running indefinitely without subscription, but the crack has a hidden backdoor that feeds user biometric data directly to an unknown third party.
definition: The state of having augmentation hardware that is currently inactive, throttled, or locked out due to lapsed subscription payments or deliberate deactivation; a common condition on the Shelf tied to poverty and corporate aug-maintenance models.
usage_example: 'Don't schedule me for anything heavy this week — I'm running dry until the 15th, chrome's all locked out till I can cover the Helion bill.'
spread: Deeply embedded in Tier 1; understood and used in Tier 2; carries stigma in Tier 3 where it is used but avoided; virtually unknown as a personal experience in Tier 4-5
